unitDescription.value: In this unit, students will explore how websites and servers work by interacting with a controlled, deliberately vulnerable web application. Through guided investigation and hands-on challenges, students will examine how data moves between a browser and server, how user input is processed, and how poor design choices can create security weaknesses. Students will test, identify and explain simple vulnerabilities in a safe learning environment, then recommend and apply improvements to make the system more secure. This unit develops practical understanding of web technologies, ethical hacking, secure design principles and responsible digital behaviour.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: The Years 9–10 cohort consists of a diverse group of boys with a wide range of digital competencies, from students with strong technical skills and personal interest in IT, to those who require further support to confidently engage with digital systems. Many students come from regional or rural backgrounds, where access to structured digital learning opportunities may have been limited. The program is designed to build on prior knowledge while introducing more advanced and applied skills relevant to future study and employment. The curriculum supports the school’s priority to equip students with transferable digital skills, critical thinking abilities, and an understanding of ethical technology use in a rapidly changing world.

description.value: Students will complete a written examination to assess their understanding of the interdependencies between hardware and software components within networked digital systems, with a focus on mechanisms for managing, controlling, and securing data access. The assessment requires students to explain the abstraction of online documents by distinguishing between content, structure, and presentation, and to justify the importance of these representations in contemporary web environments.

conditions.value: Up to 50 minutes plus 10 minutes planning time; under supervised conditions; short response up to 100 words per item, up to 600 words for the task; extended response 200–300 words per item, up to 600 words for the task

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students develop and modify innovative digital solutions, decompose real-world problems, and critically evaluate alternative solutions against stakeholder elicited user stories. Students acquire, interpret and model complex data with databases and represent documents as content, structure and presentation. They design and validate algorithms and implement them, including in an object-oriented programming language. Students explain how digital systems manage, control and secure access to data; and model cyber security threats and explore a vulnerability. They use advanced features of digital tools to create interactive content, and to plan, collaborate on, and manage agile projects. Students apply privacy principles to manage digital footprints.

moderation.value: A sample of student portfolios representing a range of achievement levels will be reviewed by another Digital Technologies teacher.

description.value: Students investigate the architecture of networked digital systems, focusing on how hardware and software components manage, control, and secure access to data. Through the analysis of a provided web application, students identify software vulnerabilities and apply their knowledge of content, structure, and presentation to propose and implement robust, secure, and user-friendly modifications. The task requires students to develop a cyber security threat model, critique the system’s digital footprint against the Australian Privacy Principles, and employ object-oriented programming to debug and harden server-side logic and input validation. Students document the problem-solving process, justifying their design choices against established criteria, user stories, and potential future enterprise impacts. The final solution is evaluated for its effectiveness in mitigating identified risks and improving overall system integrity.

conditions.value:
• Digital portfolio or equivalent
• Completed in-class under supervised conditions
• Access to provided vulnerable web application source code and documentation
• Use of approved integrated development environment (IDE) and network analysis tools
• Inclusion of a cyber security threat model, annotated code samples, and a reflective justification of modifications

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Focus on the client-server relationship and how requests are processed across a network. Students engage in discussions regarding the physical and logical components that enable web connectivity.

resources.value: Web browser developer tools, classroom demonstration of packet tracing, online simulations of the client-server model, introductory worksheet on network infrastructure.

theory.value: Students investigate how the internet functions as a network of digital systems, focusing on the roles of hardware (servers, routers, client devices) and software (browsers, web servers) in managing and transmitting data. Key terminology such as client-server model, IP address, and DNS is introduced. Students develop an understanding of how data is requested, transferred, and displayed in a web context.

prac.value: Students explore how the web works through guided simulations and demonstrations (e.g. request-response cycle). They use browser developer tools to inspect simple websites and identify basic structural elements. Introductory activities include navigating file structures and preparing a workspace for web development.

assessment.value: Formative: Teacher observation of student engagement during browser inspection activities and initial diagnostic check on network terminology.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Emphasis on the separation of content from presentation through the study of HTML semantic elements. Students begin to understand the hierarchical nature of document structure.

resources.value: Code editor (e.g., VS Code or similar), HTML starter templates, W3Schools documentation, browser live-preview tools.

theory.value: Students are introduced to how web content is structured using HTML. The concept of representing information as content and structure is explicitly taught. Students learn about common HTML elements (headings, paragraphs, images, links) and the purpose of semantic structure.

prac.value: Students begin writing basic HTML documents using a code editor. They create a simple webpage including headings, paragraphs, and images. Emphasis is placed on correct syntax, file structure, and readability of code.

assessment.value: Formative: Peer review of basic HTML structure; students verify their code displays as expected in the browser.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Introduction to the CSS box model and styling principles. Students learn how to manipulate the appearance of HTML documents without modifying the underlying source content.

resources.value: CSS cheat sheets, external style sheet templates, web design gallery for inspiration on layout, documentation on box model properties.

theory.value: Students explore the concept of presentation using CSS and how it separates design from structure. Key concepts include selectors, properties, and values, as well as the importance of consistency and maintainability in web design.

prac.value: Students extend their existing HTML pages by applying CSS styling. Tasks include changing colours, fonts, spacing, and layout. Students experiment with linking external stylesheets and modifying visual presentation without altering content.

assessment.value: Formative: Practical checklist documenting the application of CSS properties to modify an HTML template.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Explicit instruction on how web browsers parse and interpret content; comparison of uncompressed assets against compressed versions; focus on technical impacts of file size on load times.

resources.value: Online compression tools, web performance testing tools, browser developer network logs, image editing software.

theory.value: Students investigate simple data compression techniques and their importance in web communication. Concepts such as file size, load time, and efficiency are explored. Students examine examples of compressed vs uncompressed data and discuss the impact on user experience.

prac.value: Students apply optimisation techniques to their webpages, such as resizing images and reducing file sizes. They compare performance differences between optimised and non-optimised files. Activities may include using online tools to compress images and analyse file sizes.

assessment.value: Formative: Checklist of code and asset optimization progress; students document the reduction in site load times.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Consolidation and review session. Structured, scaffolded approach to revising technical concepts in preparation for the summative examination.

resources.value: Revision guides, practice examination papers, summary infographics of the client-server model, glossary of technical terms.

theory.value: Structured revision of key concepts: digital systems, HTML (content and structure), CSS (presentation), and data compression. Students consolidate their understanding through guided review and discussion.

prac.value: Revision activities including quizzes, concept mapping, and peer discussion. Students complete practice exam questions under timed conditions to build familiarity with assessment requirements.

assessment.value: Summative: Web Exam (Term 1, Week 5).

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Introduction to the server-side architecture and the concept of a vulnerable web application; students are oriented to the Grok learning platform environment for cybersecurity challenges.

resources.value: Grok Learning Web App Security module, dedicated browser sandbox environment, teacher-led walkthroughs of application architecture.

theory.value: Students examine the architecture of web applications, specifically focusing on server-side logic vs client-side display. Discussion on how poor input validation creates security gaps.

prac.value: Students commence Grok Module 1, navigating the simulated vulnerable web app to identify basic request-response patterns and recognize where untrusted input enters the server.

assessment.value: Formative: Successful completion of Grok Module 1 introductory challenges and participation in lab discussions regarding observed vulnerabilities.

outlineTheme.value: Introduction to Web Application Security (Grok Module 1)

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students map the flow of data during a standard web request. Emphasis is placed on the transition from client-side initiation to server-side processing and the security implications of this transit.

resources.value: Browser Developer Tools (Network tab), HTTP sequence diagrams, pre-configured local sandbox server environment.

theory.value: Deep dive into the HTTP request-response cycle. Students explore request methods (GET and POST), headers, and status codes. Theoretical discussion focuses on where data becomes 'untrusted' as it enters the server-side environment and the fundamental risks of improper input handling.

prac.value: Using network inspection tools, students capture and analyse live traffic from the vulnerable web app. They document the path of user data from browser input fields to server-side processing scripts, identifying potential interception or tampering points.

assessment.value: Formative: Annotated process map showing the data path and flagging potential security 'bottlenecks' or weaknesses in the transaction flow.

outlineTheme.value: The Client-Server Request-Response Cycle and Security

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Guided discovery of injection vulnerabilities. Students simulate an attacker’s perspective to observe how poorly sanitised input can manipulate backend operations.

resources.value: Cyber security lab environment, guided exploit cheat sheet, documentation on sanitisation vs validation.

theory.value: Examination of injection vulnerabilities (focusing on SQL/Command injection). Explanation of how malicious strings can alter backend logic when treated as executable code. Discussion of the 'Trust No Input' security principle.

prac.value: Students use the vulnerable web app to craft specific input strings designed to bypass authentication or extract unauthorised information. They observe the server-side results and document the system's failure to sanitise input.

assessment.value: Formative: Lab journal entries documenting successful exploit attempts and categorising the type of vulnerability identified based on input manipulation.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Introduction to cyber security threat modelling. Students transition from identifying specific flaws to understanding the broader impact of vulnerabilities on system integrity and user privacy.

resources.value: Threat modelling templates, Australian Privacy Principles (APP) summary guide, system documentation for the target web application.

theory.value: Introduction to the STRIDE threat modelling framework. Discussion of the Australian Privacy Principles (APP) regarding the storage and security of personal data. Analysis of how system weaknesses lead to data breaches.

prac.value: Students begin drafting a formal threat model for the vulnerable web application. They identify key assets (e.g., user databases) and map existing vulnerabilities to potential threats, documenting the impact on system confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

assessment.value: Formative: Initial draft of the threat model including identification of critical system vulnerabilities and their potential impacts.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Focus on the concept of 'Least Privilege' and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Students compare different access control models to understand how authentication and authorisation mechanisms govern interactions within a networked application.

resources.value: RBAC architecture diagrams, documentation on authentication vs. authorisation, access control scenario cards.

theory.value: Examination of security principles including confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA triad). Students explore access control models, discussing how administrators manage permissions for different user roles and the potential risks when these controls are misconfigured.

prac.value: Students analyse the user permission structure of the vulnerable web application. They identify where hardcoded access levels or missing session validation could allow unauthorised horizontal or vertical privilege escalation.

assessment.value: Formative: Reflection task evaluating the effectiveness of the application’s current access control against a 'Least Privilege' standard.

outlineTheme.value: Security Principles and Access Control Models

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Critiquing system design through the lens of the Australian Privacy Principles (APP). Students evaluate how the application collects, stores, and secures user data, identifying areas of non-compliance that create legal and ethical risks.

resources.value: OAIC Australian Privacy Principles summary, data collection policy templates, checklist for APP compliance.

theory.value: Deep dive into the Australian Privacy Principles, specifically focusing on data security (APP 11) and the notification of data breaches. Discussion on how digital footprints are generated by user interactions and the developer's responsibility in protecting this information.

prac.value: Students conduct a privacy audit of the web application’s input forms and database schema. They document where PII (Personally Identifiable Information) is captured and propose changes to data handling processes to align with privacy requirements.

assessment.value: Formative: Privacy audit report mapping application features to relevant Australian Privacy Principles.

outlineTheme.value: The Australian Privacy Principles in Digital Design

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Hands-on debugging session focusing on server-side logic flaws. Students work with backend code to identify where logical errors allow for input manipulation, moving beyond simple injection to more complex state-manipulation vulnerabilities.

resources.value: Backend code base (simplified Python/PHP), server-side debugging logs, input validation best-practice guides.

theory.value: Theoretical review of server-side programming concepts such as variable scope, control flow, and error handling. Students analyse the relationship between server-side decision making and system security outcomes.

prac.value: Students modify server-side scripts to implement robust input validation. They 'harden' the logic by replacing weak string comparisons with strict type checking and implementing input sanitisation functions to mitigate identified risks.

assessment.value: Formative: Code review session where students present their patches and explain how the fix improves the integrity of the server-side logic.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students transition from manual vulnerability discovery to programmatic remediation. The focus is on applying object-oriented principles to create reusable validation classes that enforce data integrity at the server boundary.

resources.value: Python/PHP object-oriented programming guides, custom validation class templates, unit test suites for verifying input sanitisation.

theory.value: Concepts of object-oriented programming (OOP) applied to security: encapsulation and data hiding. Discussion on the 'Factory' and 'Validator' patterns for sanitising user-provided data before it reaches the database. Theory of input validation vs. sanitisation.

prac.value: Students refactor existing server-side procedural scripts into a secure class structure. They develop a custom validation object to handle form submissions, ensuring all incoming data is cast to the expected type and stripped of malicious characters.

assessment.value: Formative: Code review of the custom Validator class; peer-check for coverage of expected input types.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Application of human-computer interaction (HCI) principles to secure interface design. Students learn how to provide informative feedback for invalid inputs without leaking system-level diagnostic details to potential attackers.

resources.value: UX design patterns for error states, JavaScript validation libraries, wireframing tools, documentation on secure error handling (OWASP principles).

theory.value: User experience (UX) and security trade-offs. Discussion on error handling—why explicit error messages assist attackers, and how to design friendly, non-descriptive error states for users while maintaining robust server logs.

prac.value: Students redesign the frontend form interface, implementing client-side 'soft' validation (using JavaScript) for user experience and 'hard' server-side validation for security. They create consistent error-messaging schemas.

assessment.value: Formative: Prototype interface evaluation against design criteria for usability and secure information disclosure.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Investigation into supply chain vulnerabilities, examining how third-party libraries and external dependencies can compromise the integrity of a locally secure system.

resources.value: Case studies on software supply chain breaches, dependency vulnerability scanners (e.g., Snyk, npm audit), dependency mapping templates.

theory.value: Overview of supply chain attacks. Students examine how 'hidden' code within frameworks or plugins can introduce backdoors. Discussion on auditing external dependencies and the importance of dependency management.

prac.value: Students conduct an audit of the web application’s current dependencies. They simulate a supply-chain incident by identifying a compromised library and implementing a strategy to quarantine or replace the vulnerable component.

assessment.value: Formative: Written report summarizing the dependency audit and the justification for the chosen remediation strategy.

outlineTheme.value: Supply Chain Vulnerabilities and System Integrity

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students analyse the broader implications of their secure web solutions by evaluating how robust security design creates enterprise opportunities and mitigates future digital risks.

resources.value: Case studies of enterprise security breaches, impact analysis frameworks, industry standards for cybersecurity (e.g., OWASP Top 10), and project planning templates.

theory.value: Discussion on the business value of security, including brand reputation, data trust, and regulatory compliance. Exploration of how secure design choices support long-term scalability and protect against evolving cyber threats.

prac.value: Students conduct a 'future impact' analysis of their patched web application, documenting how their security hardening (input validation and access control) protects future user data and prevents potential enterprise-level downtime.

assessment.value: Formative: Reflection entry in the portfolio comparing the 'insecure' state of the original application versus the 'secured' state in terms of long-term business and privacy risk.

outlineTheme.value: Evaluating Enterprise Opportunities and Future Impacts

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Explicit instruction on writing technical justifications for design decisions. Students learn to frame their security patches using professional terminology and evidence-based reasoning.

resources.value: Portfolio writing templates, technical writing style guides, peer-review feedback rubrics, and project documentation examples.

theory.value: Review of the criteria for the 'Fix the Vulnerable Web App' portfolio. Instruction on how to link specific coding choices (e.g., sanitisation functions, class-based validation) to the mitigation of identified threats in the original threat model.

prac.value: Drafting the justification section of the portfolio. Students map each security control implemented in the code to the specific vulnerability identified earlier in the unit, ensuring alignment with user stories and privacy principles.

assessment.value: Formative: Peer-feedback session where students read each other’s justifications to ensure logic is clear and professionally articulated.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Focus on the iterative refinement cycle—debugging code and optimising performance. Students ensure their security fixes do not negatively impact user experience.

resources.value: Code refactoring checklists, testing scripts, browser-based performance diagnostic tools, and version control best-practice notes.

theory.value: Principles of code optimisation and the trade-off between strict security measures and application performance. Reviewing efficient versus inefficient input validation patterns.

prac.value: Final debugging sprint. Students perform 'white-box' testing on their hardened applications, attempting to bypass their own fixes to verify system integrity. They optimise server-side code to improve response times without sacrificing security.

assessment.value: Formative: Final code walkthrough demonstrating the effectiveness of the fixes against a 'checklist of vulnerabilities' established in Term 1.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students undertake a final cycle of system verification, applying 'black-box' and 'white-box' testing techniques to confirm that identified vulnerabilities in the web application have been successfully mitigated. Emphasis is placed on the professional documentation of testing results, ensuring all remediation steps are clearly mapped to the original security threat model.

resources.value: White-box testing checklists, portfolio structure templates, server-side debugging logs, and peer-review feedback logs.

theory.value: Advanced discussion of testing methodologies, including unit testing for security and penetration testing logic. Students review the impact of their hardening measures on system performance and evaluate the effectiveness of their input validation against the STRIDE model.

prac.value: Students conduct comprehensive testing of their secured web application. This includes attempting to replicate previous injection and access-control exploits to verify the success of their patches. Students finalise the structure and content of their digital portfolios, documenting the 'before and after' states of the system.

assessment.value: Formative: Progress check on portfolio documentation and evidence of successful system hardening tests.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students finalise their 'Fix the Vulnerable Web App' portfolio for summative submission. The focus is on articulating the rationale behind technical choices, linking security hardening to broader enterprise risks and the Australian Privacy Principles, and presenting a professional, evidence-based technical report.

resources.value: Portfolio submission guidelines, assessment rubric, digital learning management system access, and professional formatting guides.

theory.value: Consolidation of learning regarding the lifecycle of web-based digital systems, from development and deployment to maintenance and security hardening. Reflection on the ethical responsibilities of developers regarding user data and system integrity.

prac.value: Final refinement of the portfolio, ensuring all required components are addressed: threat model, annotated code solutions, privacy audit, and justification of design choices. Submission of the completed portfolio via the school’s digital learning management system.

assessment.value: Summative: Fix the Vulnerable Web App (Portfolio).

outlineTheme.value: Final Assessment: Security Audit and Fixes Submission
